screen.title: Academic Talk: How migrating birds find their way
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in a biology class.

audio.text: Every autumn, millions of songbirds fly thousands of kilometers to their wintering grounds, and many of them travel at night, alone, on their very first journey. So how do they know which way to go? It turns out they don't rely on a single cue. They carry what amounts to several compasses.

Birds also sense the Earth's magnetic field. Interestingly, their magnetic compass doesn't distinguish north from south the way ours does. Instead, it detects the angle at which the field lines dip toward the ground, which tells a bird whether it's heading toward the pole or toward the equator. And on overcast nights, when the stars disappear, that magnetic sense appears to keep them on course.

screen.title: Academic Talk: From harpsichord to piano
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in a music history class.

audio.text: Today I want to look at an instrument you all know, the piano, and why it was such an important change. Before about 1700, the main keyboard instrument in Europe was the harpsichord. When you press a key on a harpsichord, a small hook plucks the string. The problem is that the hook plucks it in the same way no matter how hard you press, so a player can't make one note louder than another.

Around 1700, an instrument maker in Florence, Bartolomeo Cristofori, replaced the hook with a small hammer that strikes the string and then falls away. Press the key gently and the hammer hits softly; press it hard and the note is loud. That's where the name comes from: pianoforte means soft-loud in Italian.

Interestingly, the new instrument didn't catch on right away. Early pianos were quiet and expensive, and many musicians saw no reason to give up the harpsichord. It took several decades before composers began writing music that depended on gradual changes in volume. Then, in the nineteenth century, builders added iron frames, which could hold thicker strings under much greater tension. Pianos became loud enough to fill large concert halls, and that's the instrument we recognize today.

screen.title: Academic Talk: Finding planets around other stars
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an astronomy class.

audio.text: Planets orbiting other stars are extremely hard to see directly. A star is millions of times brighter than any planet near it, so the planet's faint light is simply lost in the glare. Instead, astronomers usually detect these planets indirectly, and today the most productive approach is called the transit method.

Here's the idea. If a planet's orbit happens to be lined up with our line of sight, then once per orbit the planet passes in front of its star. When that happens, it blocks a tiny fraction of the starlight, often less than one percent. A sensitive telescope that measures the star's brightness continuously will record a small, regular dip. The time between dips tells us the length of the planet's year, and the depth of each dip tells us how large the planet is compared with its star.

Now, a single dip doesn't prove anything. Stars have dark spots, and a second star passing in front can produce a similar signal. That's why astronomers want to see at least three evenly spaced dips before they take a candidate seriously. And keep in mind the method's built-in bias: it only finds systems whose orbits we happen to see edge-on, so for every planet detected this way, many more must be passing by unseen.

screen.title: Academic Talk: How bats hunt in the dark

audio.text: Today let's look at how bats find their way in complete darkness. Most bats rely on a process called echolocation. A bat produces a series of very high-pitched calls, usually too high for humans to hear, and then listens for the echoes that bounce back from objects around it. By noticing how long each echo takes to return, the bat can judge how far away an object is, and differences between what its two ears hear tell it the direction.

Now, here's what I find remarkable. When a bat is simply flying across open space, it might call around ten times per second. But as it closes in on an insect, the rate rises sharply, to well over a hundred calls per second. Researchers call this final burst the feeding buzz. The faster calls give the bat almost continuous updates about the insect's position, which matters because the insect is moving too.

Some moths, by the way, have evolved a defense. They can hear bat calls, and when they detect one, they suddenly drop or change direction. A few species even produce clicks of their own that seem to interfere with the bat's signal. So this is really an ongoing contest between hunter and prey.

audio.text: Today we're going to look at how penguins survive in some of the coldest places on Earth. First, they have a thick layer of fat under their skin. screen.title: Academic Talk: The rise of linear perspective
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an art history class.

audio.text: Let's turn to one of the great technical advances of the Renaissance: linear perspective. Before the fifteenth century, European painters certainly suggested depth. They placed distant figures higher in the picture or made them smaller, but they lacked a consistent system, and different objects in the same painting often seemed to recede at different angles.

In Florence, early in the fifteenth century, the architect Filippo Brunelleschi carried out a famous demonstration. He painted a small panel showing the city's baptistery and drilled a hole through it. A viewer looked through the hole from the back while holding a mirror in front of the panel, so the reflected painting could be compared directly with the real building. The two lined up remarkably well.

The principle behind this is that parallel lines moving away from the viewer appear to meet at a single point, which we now call the vanishing point. In the 1430s, Leon Battista Alberti described the method in writing, which allowed it to spread far beyond Brunelleschi's circle. Keep in mind, though, that perspective wasn't only about accuracy. Painters used the vanishing point to guide the viewer's eye, often toward the most important figure in the scene.

screen.title: Academic Talk: Path dependence
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an economics class.

audio.text: Let's talk about a concept economists call path dependence. The basic idea is that decisions made in the past can limit the choices available today, even when the original reasons no longer apply.

The classic example is the keyboard layout most of you are using right now, known as QWERTY. It was designed in the 1870s for mechanical typewriters. One popular explanation is that it placed common letter pairs apart so the metal arms wouldn't jam, although historians still argue about how much that really mattered. Either way, the jamming problem disappeared long ago. Other layouts have been designed since then. The Dvorak keyboard, for example, put the most common letters on the middle row, where your fingers already rest, and some people claim it's faster. Yet QWERTY is everywhere.

Why? Because once millions of people had learned it, and schools taught it, and manufacturers produced it, switching became very costly. A new layout would have to be better by enough to make everyone relearn typing at the same time. So the old standard survives, not necessarily because it's the best, but because everyone else is already using it. And economists find the same pattern whenever the value of a choice depends on what everyone else has already chosen.

screen.title: Academic Talk: Managing shared resources
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an economics class.

audio.text: In economics there's a well-known idea called the tragedy of the commons. Picture a pasture that everyone in a village may use. Each herder reasons that adding one more cow brings him the full benefit of that cow, while the cost, slightly less grass, is shared by everyone. So each herder adds cows, and eventually the pasture is ruined, even though no one wanted that outcome.

For a long time, economists assumed there were only two solutions: either the government controls the resource, or it's divided into private property. But the political economist Elinor Ostrom challenged that view. She studied fisheries, forests, and irrigation systems around the world that communities had managed successfully for centuries without either solution.

What did those communities have in common? Ostrom found that they set clear boundaries around who could use the resource, they made their own rules about how much each person could take, and, this is important, they monitored one another and applied gradually increasing penalties to people who broke the rules. In 2009 she became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in economics, partly for this work. So the lesson isn't that shared resources are always doomed. It's that the outcome depends on how the users organize themselves.

screen.title: Academic Talk: The serial position effect
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a talk in a psychology class.

audio.text: Today I want to talk about something you've probably experienced without realizing it. Imagine I read you a list of twenty words and then ask you to write down as many as you can remember. Most people recall the first few words and the last few words quite well, but the words in the middle tend to disappear. Psychologists call this the serial position effect.

So why does it happen? The words at the beginning get more rehearsal. When you hear the first word, you repeat it to yourself a few times, and that repetition helps move it into long-term memory. By the time the middle of the list arrives, you're trying to rehearse many words at once, so each one gets less attention. The words at the end are a different story. They're still sitting in short-term memory when you start writing, so you can simply read them off, so to speak.

Here's the interesting part. If I make you wait thirty seconds and count backward before you write, the advantage for the final words disappears, but the advantage for the first words remains. That tells us two different memory systems are involved. So, practically speaking, when you study, try not to always start from the same page. Otherwise the middle chapters will always get the least attention.

screen.title: Academic Talk: The wolves of Yellowstone
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an environmental science class.

audio.text: In 1995, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park after an absence of about seventy years. What happened next became one of the most famous stories in ecology. Without wolves, elk had grazed freely along the rivers, eating young willow and aspen trees before they could grow. Once wolves returned, the story goes, elk began avoiding open river valleys where they could easily be hunted. The trees recovered, beavers returned to use the wood, and their dams created ponds that supported fish and birds. Ecologists call a chain of effects like this a trophic cascade.

Now, it's a great story, and parts of it are clearly true. But more recent research suggests the picture is messier. Elk numbers also fell because of hunting by people, harsh winters, and a growing population of bears. And in some areas the willows haven't recovered at all, because without beaver dams the water table had dropped too low for the trees to grow back. In other words, removing a predator can trigger changes that simply adding it back doesn't reverse.
So what's the lesson? Not that the wolves didn't matter. They did. The lesson is that ecosystems don't always work like a light switch. Restoring one species is often only the first step.

text: Languages differ considerably in how they divide the color spectrum. Russian, for instance, obligatorily distinguishes between lighter blues (goluboy) and darker blues (siniy), whereas English speakers use a single basic term. This raises a question that has long intrigued linguists and psychologists: does the vocabulary a person habitually uses shape the way that person actually perceives the world?

Crucially, the effect vanished when participants simultaneously performed a verbal task that occupied their linguistic resources.

Researchers therefore caution against strong claims. Language does not appear to determine what people are capable of seeing; it seems instead to provide a convenient shortcut that accelerates certain judgments whenever linguistic processing is available.

text: Until the late nineteenth century, most towns set their clocks by the sun. Noon was the moment when the sun stood highest in the sky, so the time in one city could differ by several minutes from the time in a city a short distance to the east or west.

screen.title: Urban Heat Islands
text: On a summer afternoon, the center of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. Scientists call this an urban heat island. The main cause is the material that cities are built from: asphalt, concrete and brick absorb sunlight during the day and slowly release that heat at night.

Cities also lack the natural cooling that plants provide. Trees shade the ground, and they release water vapor through their leaves, which cools the surrounding air in much the same way that sweat cools skin. Where green spaces are replaced by roads and buildings, this effect disappears.

The consequences go beyond discomfort. Warmer nights prevent people from recovering from daytime heat, and heat waves in cities are linked to more hospital visits. Some cities now paint roofs white, plant trees along streets and build parks, and early results suggest that these simple changes can lower local temperatures noticeably.

screen.title: The Three-Field System
text: For many centuries, farmers across much of Europe divided their land into two large fields. Each year, one field was planted with grain, while the other was deliberately left unplanted, or fallow, so that the soil could recover its natural fertility. This method protected the soil, but it meant that half of the available land produced nothing in any given year.

Around the eighth century, many villages began organizing their land into three fields instead. One field was sown with wheat or rye in the autumn, a second was planted in spring with oats, peas, or beans, and the third was allowed to rest. The crops then rotated to a different field each year.

This change brought two significant advantages. First, two-thirds of the land was now under cultivation at any time. Second, peas and beans naturally return nitrogen to the soil, so the fields remained productive for longer. The additional oats also supported more horses, which could plow considerably faster than oxen.

screen.title: The Strength of Weak Ties
screen.directions: Read an Academic Passage — upper module
text: Sociologists distinguish between strong ties, such as those connecting close friends and relatives, and weak ties, which link acquaintances who interact only occasionally. Intuitively, one might assume that strong ties constitute the more valuable resource, since close contacts are typically more willing to offer assistance.

A frequently cited study of professional workers, however, found that people who had obtained jobs through personal contacts more often heard about the position from acquaintances than from close friends. The explanation proposed was structural: members of a tightly knit circle tend to know the same people and encounter the same information, whereas acquaintances move in different social circles and can therefore transmit news that would otherwise remain inaccessible.

Subsequent research has qualified this conclusion. Strong ties appear more influential when information is scarce or when a recommendation requires considerable trust, and the advantage of weak ties seems to depend on the type of labor market. Nevertheless, the central insight, that the value of a connection lies partly in the novelty of what it can provide, has proved remarkably durable.

text: Main Library — new loan policy

Effective March 1, the main library will replace its fixed loan periods with a demand-based system. Items with no waiting list will renew automatically up to five times, so most borrowers will no longer need to visit the desk. However, once another user places a hold on an item you have borrowed, your loan will be shortened to seven days, and you will receive an email with the new due date. Overdue fines are being abolished; instead, borrowing privileges will be suspended until held items are returned. Laptops and other equipment remain excluded from the new system.

How long people keep items will depend on whether others want them
The library will begin charging higher fines for all late returns of books

why.en: Main change (paraphrase): the loan period depends on demand. A and C contradict the text; D is equipment that is excluded.
why.tr: Ana değişiklik (parafraz): süre talebe bağlı. A ve C metnin tersi; D hariç tutulan ekipman.
why.es: Cambio principal (paráfrasis): el plazo de préstamo depende de la demanda. A y C contradicen el texto; D es material que queda excluido.

The library will send the book to the other user.

why.es: Inferencia: se suspende el derecho de préstamo en lugar de poner una multa. B es la norma antigua que se eliminó; A se aplica a los libros sin lista de espera.

To complain about the noise from the construction work next door

screen.title: Updated Course Withdrawal Policy
text: Updated Course Withdrawal Policy

Beginning this fall, students may withdraw from a course through the student portal until the end of the tenth week of the semester; previously, the limit was the eighth week. Withdrawals made after the second week will appear on the transcript as a "W," which does not affect the grade point average. Tuition is refunded in full only for withdrawals completed during the first two weeks. Students holding scholarships that require full-time enrollment should consult the Financial Aid Office before withdrawing, since dropping below twelve credits may reduce their award. After the tenth week, withdrawals are approved only in documented exceptional circumstances.

questions.stem: What is the main change described in the notice?
options: Students can no longer withdraw through the online portal
Tuition refunds will now cover the first ten weeks of a term
A "W" on the transcript will now lower the grade point average
The period for leaving a class has been extended

why.en: Main change (paraphrase): the deadline moves from the eighth to the tenth week. B mixes up the refund period with the withdrawal deadline; C contradicts "does not affect the grade point average".
why.tr: Ana değişiklik (parafraz): son tarih sekizinci haftadan onuncu haftaya kayıyor. B ücret iadesi süresini çekilme son tarihiyle karıştırıyor; C "does not affect the grade point average" bilgisiyle çelişiyor.
why.es: Cambio principal (paráfrasis): el plazo pasa de la octava a la décima semana. B confunde el periodo de reembolso con el plazo para retirarse; C contradice "does not affect the grade point average".

questions.stem: What can be inferred about a student who withdraws from a course in the fourth week?
options: The course will not appear on the student's transcript
Not all of the money they paid will be returned
The student's grade point average will be lowered
The student must provide documents explaining the decision

why.en: Inference: full refunds are given only in the first two weeks, so a fourth-week withdrawal does not qualify. A applies only to very early withdrawals (a "W" appears after week two); D describes withdrawals after the tenth week.
why.tr: Çıkarım: tam iade yalnızca ilk iki haftada yapılıyor, dördüncü haftadaki çekilme bu kapsama girmiyor. A yalnızca çok erken çekilmeler için geçerli (ikinci haftadan sonra transkriptte "W" görünür); D onuncu haftadan sonraki çekilmeleri anlatıyor.
why.es: Inferencia: el reembolso completo solo se da en las dos primeras semanas, así que retirarse en la cuarta no da derecho a él. A solo vale para retiradas muy tempranas (tras la segunda semana aparece una "W"); D describe las retiradas después de la décima semana.

questions.stem: Why should some scholarship holders contact the Financial Aid Office?
options: Their scholarships pay tuition only for the first two weeks
They are not allowed to use the student portal to withdraw
Taking fewer credits could reduce the money they receive
They need special approval to take more than twelve credits

why.en: Detail (paraphrase of "dropping below twelve credits may reduce their award"). D reverses the direction (more instead of fewer credits); A borrows the two-week refund rule.
why.tr: Ayrıntı ("dropping below twelve credits may reduce their award" ifadesinin parafrazı). D yönü tersine çeviriyor (daha az yerine daha fazla kredi); A iki haftalık iade kuralını ödünç alıyor.
why.es: Detalle (paráfrasis de "dropping below twelve credits may reduce their award"). D invierte la dirección (más créditos en vez de menos); A toma prestada la regla del reembolso de dos semanas.

Hi all, starting next week, the four digital microscopes in Room 118 must be booked through the department's online calendar instead of the paper sign-up sheet. Each booking can last up to two hours, and you may hold only one future booking at a time. If you can't use your slot, please cancel it at least a day ahead so that classmates can take it. Students who miss two bookings without cancelling will lose access for the rest of the month.
— Lena

questions.stem: Why did Lena write the email?
options: To announce that the microscopes in Room 118 will be replaced
To ask students to write their names on the paper sign-up sheet
To describe a new procedure for reserving equipment
To remind students that their lab reports are due next week

why.en: Purpose (paraphrase): the email explains the new online booking rules. B describes the old method that is being replaced; A wrongly assumes the microscopes themselves are changing.
why.tr: Amaç (parafraz): e-posta yeni çevrim içi rezervasyon kurallarını açıklıyor. B kaldırılan eski yöntemi anlatıyor; A mikroskopların değiştirileceğini sanıyor.
why.es: Propósito (paráfrasis): el correo explica las nuevas normas de reserva en línea. B describe el método antiguo que se elimina; A supone por error que se cambian los microscopios.

questions.stem: What should a student do if they cannot use a booked slot?
options: Cancel it at least one day in advance
Give the slot to a classmate
Email Lena before the session begins
Book a second slot later in the week

why.en: Detail (close to "cancel it at least a day ahead"). B misreads "so that classmates can take it": the slot is freed by cancelling, not handed over; D breaks the one-booking rule.
why.tr: Ayrıntı ("cancel it at least a day ahead" ifadesine yakın). B "so that classmates can take it" kısmını yanlış okuyor: saat iptal edilerek boşaltılır, birine devredilmez; D tek rezervasyon kuralını çiğniyor.
why.es: Detalle (cercano a "cancel it at least a day ahead"). B malinterpreta "so that classmates can take it": el turno se libera cancelándolo, no se cede; D incumple la regla de una sola reserva.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the new booking rules?
options: Bookings longer than two hours need special permission
Students who cancel twice will lose access for a month
The paper sign-up sheet can still be used in emergencies
A student cannot reserve several future sessions at once

why.en: Inference from "you may hold only one future booking at a time". B changes the rule: access is lost for missing bookings without cancelling, not for cancelling; A adds a permission that is never mentioned.

professor.name: Halvorsen
professor.post: Many universities now require students to complete an internship before they graduate. Supporters say internships teach practical skills that classes cannot. Others argue that a required internship is unfair to students who already work part-time or who cannot afford to accept an unpaid position. Should universities make an internship a graduation requirement? Why or why not?

students.name: Priya
students.post: I think they should. My cousin did an internship at an engineering firm, and she said she learned more about teamwork in three months than in two years of group projects. Employers also expect some experience now, so a requirement protects students from graduating without any.

students.name: Marcus
students.post: I disagree. I already work twenty hours a week to pay my rent, so an unpaid internship would mean losing my job. A requirement sounds fair, but it really helps students whose families can support them. Universities should encourage internships, not force them.

Others worry that if recordings are always available, fewer students will come to class, and discussions in the room will suffer. Should universities require professors to record all of their lectures? Why or why not?

students.name: Lucia
students.post: Yes, I think they should. Before my chemistry exam, I watched two lectures again, and parts I had missed the first time finally made sense. Also, many students have long commutes or part-time jobs. With a recording, missing one bus doesn't mean missing the material.

students.name: Tomas
students.post: I don't think it should be required. When my statistics professor started posting recordings, attendance dropped by almost half, and the few students who came rarely asked questions. Some professors also feel uncomfortable being recorded. Each professor should decide what works for their own course.

professor.post: Some cities have closed their historic centers to private cars, allowing only pedestrians, bicycles and public transport. Supporters say this makes city centers cleaner and more pleasant; critics argue that it hurts local businesses and makes life harder for residents. Should more cities ban private cars from their historic centers? Why or why not?

students.name: Lin
students.post: Yes. When my hometown closed its old town to cars, the streets became quieter and cafés put tables outside. More people came to walk around, so many shops actually did better than before.

students.name: Daniel
students.post: I disagree. Older people and people with disabilities often rely on cars, and buses don't reach every street. A total ban punishes the people who have the fewest alternatives.
